title: Product Opportunity Assessment
editorial_note: Opening revised to lead with the lesson itself. Remaining dialogue is an automated editorial draft; review spoken wording and meaning before final publication.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Product Opportunity Assessment.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A product opportunity describes a situation in which a defined group cannot make important progress well enough, and an organisation may be able to improve that outcome. It remains separate from the intervention so the team can compare content, policy, service, workflow, and technology responses.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: An opportunity is an unmet outcome, not a solution
turns.text: What changes when we look at an opportunity is an unmet outcome, not a solution?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A useful opportunity frame names:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: people and context: who encounters the situation and under which conditions; desired progress: what they are trying to achieve; current barrier: what prevents or degrades that progress; present behaviour: workaround, alternative, delay, abandonment, or support; consequence: what the problem costs people and the service; evidence: observations, behaviour, operations, outcomes, and uncertainty; organisational ability: assets, authority, capability, access, and strategic fit; boundary: who, when, and what is not included; success: the human outcome and service/business outcome expected to change.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: “Build a provider dashboard” is an output. “Directory owners cannot identify which consequential records are expiring before patients rely on them” is a possible opportunity. The second can be tested and may lead to a dashboard, an ownership process, an integration, or a different policy.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Assess importance, not just expressed demand
turns.text: What changes when we look at assess importance, not just expressed demand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: People request solutions using the products they know. Research should uncover the outcome beneath the request. Combine evidence:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: interviews and field observation reveal meaning, stakes, tacit work, and workarounds; behavioural and service data estimate frequency, sequence, abandonment, and variation; support and incident evidence reveal recovery cost and hidden journeys; market and alternative analysis show how people solve the problem elsewhere; operational and technical inquiry tests whether the organisation can intervene; accessibility, equity, privacy, safety, and policy review reveal who may be excluded or harmed.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Frequency alone does not determine importance. A rare failure can be critical when harm is severe. A small interaction can be strategic when it blocks the entire journey. A common annoyance may not deserve investment if an acceptable workaround exists and the organisation has little ability to improve it.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Distinguish problem evidence from solution evidence. Repeated referral failure supports the existence of a problem. Positive reaction to a concept supports one possible value proposition under test conditions. Neither proves usability, operational feasibility, adoption, or durable outcome.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at compare opportunities as portfolio choices?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use a consistent review rather than a single score that hides judgement. Examine:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: 1. importance and consequence of the unmet outcome; 2. reach and distribution across relevant groups and contexts; 3. strength, recency, and triangulation of evidence; 4. severity and reversibility of harm; 5. alternatives and present satisfaction; 6. strategic fit and organisational legitimacy; 7. ability to create a differentiated or public-service value; 8.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: data, operational, policy, and technical feasibility; 9. dependencies, lifecycle cost, and time to meaningful learning; 10. uncertainty that could overturn the bet.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Do not collapse these into arithmetic too early. Weighting is a strategy decision. A visually precise score can obscure that evidence quality differs or that one non-negotiable safety condition has failed.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: State the bet and the evidence ladder
turns.text: What changes when we look at state the bet and the evidence ladder?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Write the opportunity as a falsifiable bet:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: If we enable this group in this situation to achieve this progress, we expect this user outcome and this service or business outcome, without violating these guardrails, because this evidence suggests this mechanism.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Then define an evidence ladder:

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: problem relevance and context; current behaviour and alternatives; concept value and comprehension; interaction usability and accessibility; operational and technical feasibility; pilot adoption and workflow effect; real outcome, distribution, and durability.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Each rung answers a different uncertainty. Do not use concept enthusiasm to claim outcome or a successful build to claim value. Decide what evidence permits the bet to advance, narrow, pivot, or stop.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at avoid local optimisation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An apparent product problem may originate in policy, incentives, staffing, content ownership, or another service stage. Map upstream causes and downstream consequences.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Improving one metric can move burden elsewhere: faster automated referral may increase clinic rejection; more reminders may increase support demand; richer provider forms may transfer maintenance effort without accountability.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Opportunity assessment protects the whole journey by asking whether the organisation can change the mechanism producing the outcome, not merely add an interface near it.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at transfer example: expense management?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: “Build an AI receipt assistant” might conceal several opportunities: employees cannot understand policy before spending, extraction creates repetitive entry, managers cannot judge exceptions, or finance receives incomplete evidence. Research may show that late policy ambiguity causes most rework.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The best first intervention could be contextual policy guidance, not receipt generation.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at where this can go wrong?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Request as opportunity: a stakeholder solution enters the roadmap without an outcome frame. Market-size theatre: a large category number substitutes for reachable people and meaningful value. Frequency dominance: common low-impact friction displaces rare but severe exclusion or risk.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Evidence blending: problem, concept, usability, feasibility, and outcome evidence are treated as interchangeable. Strategic wish: organisational desire is presented as user evidence. Feasibility blind spot: policy, data, staffing, or lifecycle constraints arrive after commitment. Scorecard false precision: weighted numbers hide uncertainty and non-negotiable guardrails.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Opportunity hoarding: branches remain “priorities” after evidence weakens them.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Senior product designers help decide what not to build. They make opportunity cost visible, expose the assumption that could overturn a bet, distinguish evidence strength from stakeholder confidence, and preserve high-consequence minority needs against roadmap averaging. They involve operations and policy early enough that desirability is not judged in an imaginary service.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: An opportunity is ready for commitment when the team can name the affected outcome, mechanism, evidence, boundary, ability to intervene, next uncertainty, and conditions for stopping—not when every uncertainty has disappeared.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: <! -- Editorial: manual revision; curated product example --

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Illustrative scenario: a restaurant booking product. The team proposes a waitlist feature. Opportunity assessment asks which diners and restaurants face the problem, how often it occurs, what alternatives they use, whether the service can honour a promised place, and what outcome would justify investment. A popular feature request is not yet evidence of a viable opportunity.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Open a product roadmap or release announcement. Replace each feature name with the human outcome it is supposed to improve. Can you identify the present barrier, affected group, evidence, and success signal? If several different features claim the same vague outcome, the roadmap may be organising outputs rather than opportunities.
